paper_metadata.title: Solving Linear Systems on Quantum Hardware with Hybrid HHL++

summary: The paper demonstrates Hybrid HHL++ on Quantinuum H-series trapped-ion hardware for small portfolio-optimization linear systems, using 2-asset instances on hardware and 6-asset instances in scaling studies. Key reported numbers include 3-, 4-, and 5-bit semiclassical QPE fidelities of 98.1±1.4%, 95.0±1.6%, and 43.2±1.0%, and a reduced HHL validation circuit with 10 qubits and 262±19.36 ZZPhase-depth in Table 3; the authors explicitly state they do not claim asymptotic speedup.

experiments.description: Hybrid HHL++ on Quantinuum trapped-ion hardware for small-scale mean-variance portfolio optimization, including spectral scaling, semiclassical QPE benchmarking, and HHL solution validation via controlled-SWAP.

algorithm.variant: Hybrid HHL++ with spectral scaling and semiclassical QPE

problem_sizes: 6 assets (8x8 linear system, future scaling study)

algorithm.parameter_initialization: Initial gamma guess from an overestimate of lambda_max; eigenvalue estimates obtained from semiclassical QPE output distribution

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Mean-variance portfolio optimization is reformulated as a Hermitian linear system Ax=b; solution state encodes portfolio weights
problem_formulation.objective_function: minimize w^T Σ w subject to p^T w = ξ and r^T w = μ

problem_instance.description: Portfolio optimization using S&P 500 assets; main hardware experiments use 2 assets (4x4 system), with additional scaling analysis for 6 assets (8x8 system)

dataset_specification.description: Historical covariance matrix, expected returns, and prices derived from S&P 500 assets; 2-asset instances for hardware experiments

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Constructed linear system from portfolio optimization formulation; details of covariance/return/price estimation not further specified
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Multiple problem instances: six 2-asset instances for hardware/emulator/simulation comparisons; five instances for HHL validation; four 6-asset instances for noise-scaling study; fidelity via bootstrap (9,999 resamples) and inner product via controlled-SWAP test

noise_model.noise_type: hardware noise; emulator with approximated noise; two-qubit fault probability p2 varied in emulator

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Classical computation of U=e^{2πiγA}, eigenvalue estimates, and rotation angles; classical loading of analytical solution for SWAP test
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Fidelity computation with bootstrap resampling; inner product from measured ancilla probabilities

speedup_claims.conditions: The paper explicitly states no asymptotic speedup is claimed.
speedup_claims.caveats: Hybrid HHL++ is presented as an application-oriented benchmark and near-term demonstration, not a speedup result.

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Hybrid HHL++ on 2-asset portfolio instances; 10 qubits reported for the reduced HHL validation circuit; ZZPhase depth 262±19.36 in Table 3 and 964 for the 6-asset HHL in Table 4.
limiting_factors: No asymptotic speedup claimed in the paper
Classical preprocessing is substantial, including classical Hamiltonian simulation and eigenvalue estimation
Problem sizes are tiny (2 assets / 4x4 system on hardware)
Performance is evaluated against noiseless simulation and classical analytical solutions, not against a strong classical solver benchmark
Noise and circuit depth remain limiting for scaling

notes: num_qubits=10 taken from Table 3 for the reduced HHL circuits; this includes the HHL output and ancilla registers used in the validation experiment.

circuit_depth not given as a generic depth for exp_1; paper reports ZZPhase depth values for subcircuits (e.g., 262±19.36 in Table 3, 63±4.60 for 4-bit semiclassical QPE, 964 for 6-asset HHL in Table 4).
speedup_order set to none because the paper explicitly states no asymptotic speedup is claimed.
The authors explicitly state they do not claim speedup and present the work as an application-oriented benchmark.
Hardware results are high-fidelity but do not establish quantum advantage over classical methods.
